opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that if you just look at aggregate metrics like perplexity, or performance on a big benchmark, you can't really tell *why* the model is doing well. Natural text is full of shortcuts. Most of the time the simple heuristic and the correct structural rule make the same prediction, so a model can look very good without having learned the structure at all.

So the approach I've found most useful is what you might call targeted evaluation, which borrows heavily from psycholinguistics. You design minimal pairs, two sentences that differ in one controlled way, where one is grammatical and one isn't, and you ask whether the model prefers the grammatical one. Subject-verb agreement is the classic case: "The keys to the cabinet *are* on the table" versus "*is* on the table." If the model is just tracking the nearest noun, it'll get that wrong. If it's tracking the actual syntactic subject, it'll get it right. Then you can make it harder with relative clauses, attractors, and so on, and see where things break down.

Another piece I care about is generalization, specifically out-of-distribution generalization. Humans don't just do well on sentences that look like what they've heard before. We generalize in systematic ways to new combinations. So I like evaluations where training and test differ in a principled way. For example, you train on data that's ambiguous between a linear rule and a hierarchical rule, like question formation in English, and see which rule the model infers. That tells you about the model's inductive biases, not just its ability to fit the data.

I'd also add a caveat. A lot of these tests are behavioral, and I think behavior is the right place to start, because that's what we ultimately care about. But behavior alone doesn't tell you *how* the model gets there. That's where interpretability methods come in: probing, causal interventions on internal representations, and so on. Ideally you'd combine the two. Show the model behaves correctly, then show that the behavior depends on something that looks like a structural representation, and not on some correlate that happens to work on your test set.

Finally, I think it's worth being honest about the comparison to humans. Humans make agreement errors too, in particular contexts. So the question isn't only "is the model perfect?" but "does it make the same kinds of errors people do, and does it learn from a comparable amount of data?" That second question, data efficiency, is one I think is really underappreciated. Current models see vastly more text than a child ever does. So even when they succeed on these tests, that doesn't necessarily tell us much about how humans acquire language.

r001.rationale: The response says models can succeed through shortcuts without learning structure, but it does not identify memorized local word sequences as the shortcut.

r002.rationale: It recommends minimal-pair agreement evaluations in which choosing the grammatical verb depends on tracking the syntactic subject rather than a nearby noun.

r003.rationale: It explicitly links targeted evaluation to psycholinguistics and describes minimal pairs that vary one controlled factor to test the ability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version of my answer is that we should evaluate them the way psycholinguists evaluate people: with controlled experiments designed to isolate a specific linguistic generalization, rather than with aggregate performance on naturally occurring text.

The problem with just looking at perplexity or at accuracy on a benchmark like, say, a natural language inference dataset is that those numbers mix together a lot of things. A model can get a high score by exploiting statistical regularities that have nothing to do with syntax. If the task is "does the subject agree with the verb," and in the training data the noun closest to the verb is usually the subject, then a model that just looks at the nearest noun will look great most of the time. You'd never know it had learned the wrong rule.

So what we did, starting with the work with Emmanuel Dupoux and Yoav Goldberg, was to construct minimal pairs where the heuristic and the real syntactic rule diverge. Take a sentence like "the keys to the cabinet are on the table." The attractor, "cabinet," is singular, and it sits right next to the verb. If the model prefers "is" there, it's tracking the linear neighbor. If it prefers "are," it has, at least in this case, done something that looks like tracking hierarchical structure. And then you vary the distance, the number of attractors, relative clauses, and so on, and you see where it breaks.

A few principles come out of that. One is that you want to test on things the model is unlikely to have seen verbatim, which is increasingly hard with web-scale pretraining, so synthetic or templated test sets are actually a feature, not a bug. Another is that you want the evaluation to be targeted. "Does the model understand syntax" is not a well-formed question. "Does the model generalize subject-verb agreement across a relative clause" is. A third, which I think gets neglected, is that you should compare the model to humans doing the same task under similar conditions. Humans make agreement attraction errors too. If the model's error profile looks like the human one, that's informative in a different way than if it's just failing randomly.

And then there's the generalization question that I think matters most. The interesting test isn't whether the model gets the common cases right, it's whether it extrapolates in a structure-sensitive way to cases that are underdetermined by the training data. The classic example is question formation. If you only ever see simple sentences, do you learn "move the first auxiliary" or "move the auxiliary of the main clause"? Those make identical predictions on the training data and opposite predictions on the test. That's the kind of thing we can set up deliberately, and it tells you something about the model's inductive biases rather than just its capacity to memorize.

I'd also say we should be careful about the word "understand." I try to avoid claims about understanding and instead ask whether the model's behavior is consistent with a particular generalization, and whether its internal representations encode that structure in a way we can detect with probing or causal interventions. Behavior and representations can come apart, and both are worth looking at. But if the behavior isn't systematic, I don't think any amount of probing should convince us.

r001.rationale: It explains that a model can score well by relying on local cues, such as the nearest noun, while applying the wrong syntactic rule.

r002.rationale: It recommends minimal pairs where local heuristics and syntactic structure predict different verb forms, making structure-sensitive prediction testable.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends controlled experiments modeled on psycholinguistic evaluation to isolate a specific linguistic generalization.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to be more precise about what we mean by understanding linguistic structure. A model can do very well at predicting words, or even on a particular benchmark, without using the kind of generalization that we’re interested in. So I would start with a specific hypothesis about what the model has learned and design an experiment that distinguishes that hypothesis from simpler alternatives.

Take subject–verb agreement. If you give a model “The key to the cabinets,” does it expect “is” or “are”? The relevant noun is “key,” even though “cabinets” is closer to the verb. That lets us ask whether the model’s predictions reflect the structure of the sentence or just something like agreement with the most recent noun. And you want to vary those factors systematically, rather than look at a few examples that happen to work.

Of course, getting that distinction right doesn’t establish that the model understands language in some broad sense. It’s evidence for a particular ability. You also want to test whether that ability generalizes to unfamiliar words and constructions, and examine where it breaks down. For me, the goal is an explanation of what the model has learned, rather than a single score that we label “understanding.”

r001.rationale: The response says word prediction may succeed without the desired generalization and contrasts structural knowledge with a recent-noun heuristic, but it does not state that success can come from memorized local word sequences.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing subject–verb agreement in sentences like “The key to the cabinets,” where the correct prediction depends on identifying the structurally relevant noun rather than following the closest noun.

r003.rationale: It recommends varying factors systematically and designing experiments to distinguish hypotheses, but does not connect this approach to psychological experiments or say to hold other factors constant.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to move beyond asking whether a model does well on some broad benchmark and ask what hypotheses that success lets us rule out. A model can get the right answer using a superficial cue, so we need experiments where that cue and the linguistic structure make different predictions.

Take subject–verb agreement. If you have a sentence like “The key to the cabinets is on the table,” the verb agrees with “key,” even though “cabinets” is closer to it. We can systematically vary those intervening nouns and see whether the model tracks the grammatical subject or just the most recent noun. And we should compare minimally different sentences so that we have a clear idea of what’s driving the result.

But even success on that experiment doesn’t establish that the model understands language in some general sense. You want converging evidence across constructions, and you want to test whether it generalizes to combinations it hasn’t encountered during training. I’d treat evaluation as a program of controlled experiments: specify the structural knowledge you’re interested in, identify alternative strategies, and design tests that distinguish between them.

r001.rationale: It says a model may use superficial cues, such as the most recent noun, but does not state that successful next-word prediction can rely on memorized local word sequences.

r002.rationale: The subject–verb agreement example varies intervening nouns to test whether the model predicts based on grammatical structure or the nearest noun.

r003.rationale: It recommends controlled experiments and minimally different sentences, but does not connect this approach to psychological experiments.
